data.text:
Does _strip_heredocs treat a quoted <<EOF as a real heredoc, hiding a next-line command?
A quoted <<EOF is literal, not an opener; the next line is a command that must be refused.
_strip_heredocs regex-matches << per line without quote awareness, so '<<EOF' inside a quote opens a heredoc and drops the supposed body (git push) before the scan.

evidence.note: CONFIRMED via probe: unfixed HEAD FB.check("echo '<<EOF'\ngit push origin main\nEOF") -> None (forbidden git push missed); after making _strip_heredocs quote-aware -> Refusal entry 'git push' (recorded on bug Bdd23c77383).
claim guidance returned r-task-phase-needs-wave, r-gemini-key-load and the D-* decisions governing this item; rule of note: load GEMINI_API_KEY before gemini reviewer gates.

ddflow/services/forbidden.py _strip_heredocs is now quote-aware (_heredoc_openers); regression test tests/test_forbidden_commands.py::test_a_quoted_heredoc_marker_is_not_a_heredoc added; commit e10ca9176.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new quote tracker starts a quote state from any unescaped `'` or `"`, even when that quote is inside a shell comment. Given the valid command text `# don't run
cat <<EOF
git push origin main
EOF`, the first line contains an apostrophe in a comment, so `_heredoc_openers` returns `quote = "'"` for that line. On the next line `cat <<EOF`, the scanner is still in single-quote mode, so the real `<<EOF` opener is not recorded; `_strip_heredocs` therefore leaves the heredoc body line `git push origin main` in the stripped text. That line is heredoc data, not a command, so the forbidden check can falsely refuse a valid command. The quote state must ignore comment text (or comments must be lexically removed before quote tracking).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_heredoc_openers

data.probe:
Fix: _heredoc_openers now skips a comment to end of line (a '#' at a comment boundary), so a quote inside a comment no longer leaves a dangling quote state; tests/test_forbidden_commands.py::test_a_quoted_heredoc_marker_is_not_a_heredoc adds '# don't run
cat <<EOF
git push origin main
EOF' -> None

chunk_findings.detail: The new comment shortcut treats `#` as a comment whenever the immediately preceding character is in `_COMMENT_BOUNDARY`, but that character may be escaped and therefore not a real word boundary. The backslash branch skips the escaped character, so the escaped boundary remains visible as `line[i - 1]`. For the valid command text `echo foo\ #" <<X` / `cat <<X "` / `git push origin main` / `X`, the backslash escapes the space before `#`, so the `#` is not a comment and the following `"` opens a double-quoted string that continues to the closing quote on the second line; consequently the `<<X` tokens are quoted data and `git push` on the third line is a command that must be reported. Because the scanner jumps to end of line at the `#`, it never records the opening quote, sees line 2 as unquoted, records `<<X` as a heredoc opener, strips the `git push` line as heredoc body, and `_check` returns None instead of finding the forbidden command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_heredoc_openers (new `#` branch)

chunk_findings.detail:
The diff removes the old `elif quote == '"':` state handler but still lets `_dquote_end` return `('"', n)` when a double quote is left open. On the next call, `_heredoc_openers` only special-cases `quote == "'"`, so a line that is still inside a double-quoted string is scanned as unquoted. For the valid shell input:

```sh
echo "
<<EOF"
git push
EOF
```

the first line leaves `quote == '"'`. On the second line, the current code reaches the `<`/`<<` branch and `_HEREDOC.match(line, 0)` matches `<<EOF` even though that text is literal inside the still-open double quote. The returned opener causes `_strip_heredocs` to treat `git push` as heredoc body and strip it, so the forbidden guard can return no finding. The same missing state handling also misinterprets a leading closing quote such as `"; <<EOF` as an opening quote, because `_dquote_end` always treats the quote at `i` as opening.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_heredoc_openers

chunk_findings.detail:
`_dquote_close` returns `n` both when a double quote remains open to end-of-line and when it closes on the last character, but the new callers in `_heredoc_openers` interpret `j == n` as “still open”. Thus a double-quoted string that ends exactly at the line end leaves a bogus open quote state. Given the script:
```sh
echo ""
foo " <<EOF"
git push origin main
EOF
```
line 1 closes its empty quoted argument at the last character, yet the scanner remains in `quote == '"'`. On line 2 it treats the opening quote of ` " <<EOF"` as the closing quote, then scans the following ` <<EOF"` as unquoted, records a heredoc, and strips the next line. `_check` returns `None` even though `git push origin main` is a real command, not heredoc body, reintroducing the forbidden-command hiding this change was meant to fix.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_heredoc_openers

chunk_findings.detail:
The new quote scanner treats the closing quote of a quoted heredoc delimiter as the start of a shell string quote. `_HEREDOC` matches forms like `<<'EOF'` or `<<"EOF"` but stops before the closing delimiter quote, so `_heredoc_openers` later sees that closing quote while `quote == ""` and sets `quote` to `'` or `"`. `_strip_heredocs` does not clear that state after skipping the heredoc body. For input:
```sh
cat <<'EOF'
safe
EOF
cat <<EOF
git push
EOF
```
the first real heredoc body is stripped, but the closing `'` in `<<'EOF'` leaves `quote == "'"`. The next line `cat <<EOF` is then considered inside a single quote, its marker is not returned, and `git push` remains in the stripped output. A forbidden-command check on this text will flag `git push` even though it is heredoc data.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_heredoc_openers

chunk_findings.detail:
The new regex still matches only a prefix of a quoted here-document delimiter when the delimiter contains characters outside its delimiter character class. Shell allows a quoted here-document delimiter to contain whitespace, so `cat <<'EOF with spaces'` is a valid here-document whose delimiter is `EOF with spaces`. `_HEREDOC` matches only `<<'EOF` (group 2 is `EOF`) because group 2 excludes whitespace and the optional `\1?` cannot reach the closing quote. `_strip_heredocs` then searches for a later line whose stripped text equals `EOF`; given the valid script:
```sh
cat <<'EOF with spaces'
EOF with spaces
git push origin main
EOF
```
the real delimiter line is line 1, so `git push origin main` is an actual command after the here-document ends. The guard instead finds the later `EOF` line, skips everything up to it, and returns `None`, hiding the forbidden command. The added regression test only covers `<<'EOF'`, where the closing quote immediately follows a simple delimiter, so it does not exercise this case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_HEREDOC

chunk_findings.detail:
The new bare delimiter branch `(\S+)` greedily includes shell operators that end the delimiter word. Given the input `cat <<EOF; safe
EOF
git push origin main
EOF;`, the regex captures the delimiter as `EOF;` instead of `EOF`; `_strip_heredocs` then searches for a terminator line equal to `EOF;`, finds the final line, and skips the intervening `git push origin main` line. The new bare delimiter class treats a quote as ending the delimiter word, but in shell a quote after an unquoted prefix starts a quoted segment that is part of the delimiter. Given input `cat <<safe'end'
safeend
git push origin main
safe`, the regex captures the delimiter as `safe` instead of the shell delimiter `safeend`; `_strip_heredocs` then skips the real terminator `safeend`, strips the following `git push origin main` line as heredoc body, and stops at the later `safe` command line, so the guard returns None even though `git push origin main` is a separate forbidden command after the real heredoc terminator.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new double-quote branch inside the delimiter word does not perform shell quote removal for backslash escapes inside a double-quoted delimiter. For the shell line `cat <<"a\"b"`, the here-doc delimiter after quote removal is `a"b`, but `_heredoc_word` treats the backslash as ordinary text, appends it, and stops at the escaped `"` as if it were the closing quote, producing a delimiter such as `a\b`. The call site records this delimiter and `_strip_heredocs` then skips following lines until it sees that exact delimiter. Given:
```sh
cat <<"a\"b"
git push origin main
a"b
git push origin main
```
the real terminator `a"b` does not match the scanner's `a\b`, so the scanner skips the terminator and the following `git push origin main` command as heredoc body, causing the forbidden-command check to return `None` instead of refusing.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_heredoc_word

chunk_findings.detail:
The new quote scanner treats the closing quote of a quoted heredoc delimiter as the start of a shell string quote. `_HEREDOC` matches forms like `<<'EOF'` or `<<"EOF"` but stops before the closing delimiter quote, so `_heredoc_openers` later sees that closing quote while `quote == ""` and sets `quote` to `'` or `"`. `_strip_heredocs` does not clear that state after skipping the heredoc body. For input:
```sh
cat <<'EOF'
safe
EOF
cat <<EOF
git push
EOF
```
the first real heredoc body is stripped, but the closing `'` in `<<'EOF'` leaves `quote == "'"`. The next line `cat <<EOF` is then considered inside a single quote, its marker is not returned, and `git push` remains in the stripped output. A forbidden-command check on this text will flag `git push` even though it is heredoc data.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_heredoc_openers

chunk_findings.detail:
The new regex still matches only a prefix of a quoted here-document delimiter when the delimiter contains characters outside its delimiter character class. Shell allows a quoted here-document delimiter to contain whitespace, so `cat <<'EOF with spaces'` is a valid here-document whose delimiter is `EOF with spaces`. `_HEREDOC` matches only `<<'EOF` (group 2 is `EOF`) because group 2 excludes whitespace and the optional `\1?` cannot reach the closing quote. `_strip_heredocs` then searches for a later line whose stripped text equals `EOF`; given the valid script:
```sh
cat <<'EOF with spaces'
EOF with spaces
git push origin main
EOF
```
the real delimiter line is line 1, so `git push origin main` is an actual command after the here-document ends. The guard instead finds the later `EOF` line, skips everything up to it, and returns `None`, hiding the forbidden command. The added regression test only covers `<<'EOF'`, where the closing quote immediately follows a simple delimiter, so it does not exercise this case.

chunk_findings.detail: The change in `_heredoc_name` attempts to handle backslash escapes inside double-quoted heredoc delimiters by checking `if q == '"' and line[i] == "\\" and i + 1 < n:`. However, inside a double-quoted string in shell (POSIX bash/sh), backslashes only escape specific characters (`$`, `` ` ``, `"`, `\`, and newline). For other characters (such as an arbitrary letter or quote like `a\"b`), the backslash is preserved literally. For the shell line `cat <<"a\"b"`, the backslash escapes the double quote, so the delimiter name is `a"b`. But with the implementation: `i` starts at the first character inside the quotes, which is `a`. Then `\` is encountered. Because it is followed by `"`, it strips the backslash and appends `"`, terminating the inner loop early at the closing quote (or failing to parse correctly), producing the wrong delimiter name `a` or `a` instead of `a"b`. Given input `cat <<"a\"b"\ngit push\na"b`, `_heredoc_name` parses the delimiter incorrectly, treats subsequent lines as part of the heredoc, and fails to detect the forbidden command.

chunk_findings.detail:
The changed double-quote escape set omits newline, but in shell double quotes a backslash also escapes a newline (line continuation). `_heredoc_name` does not stop at newlines inside quotes, so it can be called on a quoted delimiter word containing a backslash-newline, e.g. the string `cat <<"a\` newline `b"`. At the backslash, `line[i + 1]` is `
`, so the new condition is false; the code appends the backslash and then the newline, returning a delimiter like `a\
b` instead of the shell delimiter `ab`. A here-doc terminator match using that delimiter will fail to stop at the real terminator and can skip subsequent command lines.
